patient_information: A 24-year-old Malawian businessman who tested positive for HIV a week prior to presentation and had not yet started antiretroviral medication. His CD4 count was 134 cells/μL.
chief_complaint: Dark spots on his arm and leg for one month, facial swelling, and a three-month history of cough and worsening shortness of breath.
history_of_present_illness: For the last month, the patient noticed progressive dark spots on his arm and leg, leading to facial swelling. Concurrently, he reported a 3-month history of a cough productive of white sputum and worsening shortness of breath. He denied constitutional symptoms of weight loss, fevers, or night sweats and had no history of previous tuberculosis.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a businessman from Malawi. His wife was also HIV-positive but not on antiretroviral therapy, and his two children, aged 6 and 4, had not yet been tested for HIV.
vitals: Temperature was 36°C (96.8°F), respiratory rate was 32 breath cycles per minute, and pulse was 102 bpm.
physical_exam: The patient was comfortable at rest with moderate facial oedema. Examination revealed widespread dark-purplish plaques on the skin and palate. The respiratory exam showed decreased air entry and dullness at the right lung base. His right leg was swollen from the foot to the knee with prominent, coalescing dark plaques. The rest of the physical examination was normal.
labs_and_diagnostics: The patient was newly diagnosed with HIV with a CD4 count of 134 cells/μL. His hemoglobin was 10.2 g/dL and MCV was 88.4 fL. Sputum microscopy and GeneXpert tests were negative for tuberculosis. A chest radiograph showed bilateral patchy opacifications in the lower and mid zones of the lungs with peribronchovascular changes. A bronchoscopy was attempted but failed.
differential_diagnosis: The main differential diagnoses were tuberculosis and Kaposi's sarcoma (KS). Tuberculosis was considered due to the patient's HIV status and chronic cough. The skin and palatal lesions were typical for Kaposi's sarcoma, raising suspicion of pulmonary involvement. Dual pathology with both TB and KS was also considered a possibility.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient did not improve with a short course of oral antibiotics. He was referred to start antiretroviral medication (ART) and palliative chemotherapy for presumed pulmonary Kaposi's sarcoma.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is disseminated Kaposi's sarcoma (KS), an HIV-associated malignancy caused by human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8). The diagnosis was made clinically based on the characteristic widespread dark-purplish cutaneous and palatal plaques in a newly diagnosed, ART-naïve HIV-positive patient with a low CD4 count (134 cells/μL). Pulmonary involvement was strongly suspected given his respiratory symptoms and typical chest radiograph findings after tuberculosis was excluded by negative sputum and GeneXpert tests.
